newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: New Zealand markets rally despite unclear result.
newsitem.headline: New Zealand markets rally despite unclear result.

text.p: New Zealand markets rallied sharply on Monday despite an inconclusive general election, relieved at a poor showing by the high-tax, big-spending left-wing Alliance.
Prime Minister Jim Bolger had warned of "Sunday, bloody Sunday" and the "Crash of '97" if New Zealanders voted in a government of the left.
His National Party and its allies won 53 seats against the 50 for the two left-wing parties, Labour and the Alliance, leaving nationalist New Zealand First with 17 seats and the balance of power.

The New Zealand dollar jumped nearly one U.S. cent to 70 U.S. cents in busy morning busines. The share market rallied 0.9 percent to 2,270.28, a few points shy of a 2-1/2 year high. Bonds rallied strongly, yields falling around 15 basis points.
Finance Minister Bill Birch said markets had acted maturely and knew there would be a hiatus before a government was formed.

"There is a pretty strong appreciation in the markets about the role of the caretaker government... During the caretaker period nothing changes, the policies simply continue as they are while negotiations...continue," he told Reuters.

Asked about the possibility of prolonged political stalemate, Birch said: "I can understand the market's apprehension about that but I think the election result indicated strong support for the direction in which the economy is going."

The key election outcome for markets was the poor showing of the Alliance, with only 10 percent of the vote. Alliance policies included big tax increases, higher import tariffs and major changes to the central bank framework.
"The positive thing was that the Alliance, which was the only party which could really cause damage, were taken out of play, said National Bank chief dealer Stu Nattrass.

"There shouldn't be any shocks. There were no surprises about this result. If people hadn't put this result into their calculations then I don't know what they were doing," said Bankers Trust foreign exchange dealer Philip Lindberg.
Nattrass said he was surprised at the strength of the kiwi dollar and doubted it would be sustained, particularly if New Zealand First opted to go with Labour, as was most likely.
Lindberg said the foreign exchange market was prepared to live with uncertainty for up to six weeks.
The market had acted with relief and was anticipating a return of offshore interest via eurokiwi and samurai bond issues, said Westpac Head of Financial Markets Chris Rand.
Rand doubted the Alliance would now be in a position to extract large concessions from the more moderate Labour Party.

"They really don't have that same sort of leverage and that certainly makes the market feel more comfortable," Rand said. "The basic economic policy of NZ First isn't too far removed from either Labour or National."
International credit rating agency Standard & Poor's soothed markets by saying it was comfortable with the election result.
"Broadly speaking, we are comfortable with the types of scenarios that we can perceive going forward," Sovereign Risk Managing Director David Beers told Reuters on Sunday.

"It is broadly consistent with what we have been saying, which is we did not think if there was going to be a change of government that it would necessarily portend a substantial deviation from existing policy settings," he said.
